extracted.intended_audience: professional astronomers, observatory directors, and researchers planning large-scale stellar/astrometric programmes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and methodological standards for large-scale astrometric and spectroscopic programmes to determine stellar proper motions, parallaxes, radial velocities, magnitudes, and spectral types, and for the planning of observatory resources to support those programmes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of observed proper motion
rubrics_metrics.description: What we call the observed proper motion of a star has three possible sources of origin: (1) the parallactic motion (effect of the Sun's motion through space), (2) the peculiar or particular motion of the star (its own absolute motion in space), (3) that part due to inevitable error of observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing or interpreting proper motions, explicitly decompose observed motion into these three contributions; account for solar/parallactic component, intrinsic stellar motion, and measurement error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption of random peculiar motions when determining solar motion
rubrics_metrics.description: In discussions of the solar motion it has been assumed that the peculiar motions of the stars are arranged at random and may therefore be considered zero in the mean for a considerable number of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption permits finding a value for precession and a common apex for the solar motion leaving residual peculiar motions with mean zero — but its validity should be examined for the sample used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of parallax for rigorous determination of the Sun's motion
rubrics_metrics.description: To proceed rigorously, and especially to determine the amount as well as the direction of the Sun's motion in space, we ought to know the parallax of every star employed in the discussion, as well as its proper motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying solely on magnitude-based distance assumptions when determining solar motion; secure direct parallax measurements for stars used in such determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity of assuming equal absolute luminosity across magnitudes/regions
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption that stars of a particular magnitude are roughly at the same distance (derived from hypothesis that on average they all have equal absolute luminosity) is not legitimate: (1) because of extreme differences in absolute luminosity of stars, (2) because it implies the average absolute luminosity is the same in all regions of space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use simple magnitude-class as a proxy for distance without direct parallax evidence; check for luminosity variation and regional differences before inferring distances from apparent magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallax measurement demands long series and finest instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate parallaxes (as historically shown by Henderson, Struve, Bessel, etc.) required minute sifting of numerical results, long series of observations, and the finest instruments of the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan parallax programmes with long observational baselines and the highest-precision instruments available; expect that determining accurate parallaxes will be laborious and time-consuming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of using apparent parallactic motions from the Sun's motion as a parallax probe
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea is suggested: why should not the apparent parallactic motions of the stars, as produced by the Sun's motion in space, be utilised as a means of determining stellar parallax?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether solar-motion-induced apparent parallactic effects can be exploited to infer parallaxes, but evaluate limitations and biases before wide adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating stellar density requires accounting for interstellar absorption and luminosity ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot determine absolute star-density because intrinsically faint stars, if removed to greater distance, would fall below observational magnitude limits; an estimate requires assuming faint and bright stars are distributed similarly and knowledge of absorption of light through interstellar space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating stellar density vs distance, include corrections/uncertainties for interstellar absorption and test the assumption that the ratio of intrinsically faint to bright stars is constant across space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate determinations by region/magnitude/proper motion/spectral type
rubrics_metrics.description: The velocity and direction of the Sun's motion may be treated as constants for many centuries and may be separately determined from groups of stars of various regions, magnitudes, proper motions, and spectral types; differences not attributable to observational error must indicate a common velocity or direction of motion of that group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse subsamples (by galactic region, magnitude, motion, spectral type) separately to detect group motions or systematic differences rather than assuming homogeneity across all samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of long time-baseline for proper motions (value grows as square of age)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations for proper motion increase in value as the square of their age, whereas measurements for velocity in line of sight, parallax, magnitude, and spectrum type may be made at any time without loss of value for broad cosmical purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise and preserve long-term astrometric programmes (long baselines) for proper motion studies; do not sacrifice long-term proper-motion observations for short-term acquisition of other data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meridian plate-to-absolute-position conversion requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: There is still needed the accurate meridian observation of some eight or ten stars on each photographic plate so as to permit the conversion of the relative star-places on the plate into absolute star-places in the heavens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every astrographic plate has accurate meridian observations of ~8–10 reference stars to tie relative photographic positions to an absolute reference frame; treat this as essential for future re-use of the plates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination and sufficiency of observatories for meridian work
rubrics_metrics.description: Three observatories in each hemisphere should be sufficient; the quality of the work should be of the best, and quality should not be sacrificed for speed of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organise meridian programmes with at least three well-coordinated observatories per hemisphere and enforce high-quality standards rather than rushing quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kapteyn programme principle: symmetrically distributed areas with complete data
rubrics_metrics.description: Kapteyn's programme is based on the principle that adequate data as to proper motions, parallaxes, magnitudes, and the type of spectrum of stars situated in limited but symmetrically distributed areas of the sky will suffice to determine many of the broader facts of the constitution of the universe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design surveys that collect complete multi-parameter datasets (proper motion, parallax, magnitude, spectrum) in symmetrically distributed sky patches rather than only scattered measurements, to permit robust inference of global structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radial velocities must be determined star by star; no satisfactory wholesale method
rubrics_metrics.description: All present experience shows that there is no known satisfactory method of determining radial velocity of stars by wholesale methods, but that such velocities must be determined star by star.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan radial-velocity programmes anticipating per-star spectroscopic work; do not rely on bulk shortcuts; allocate telescope/time resources accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumentation requirement for faint-star radial velocities
rubrics_metrics.description: For the fainter stars, huge telescopes and spectroscopes of comparatively low dispersion must be employed for determining velocities in the line of sight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide access to very large-aperture reflectors and appropriate low-dispersion spectrographs when aiming to obtain radial velocities for faint stars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for large reflecting telescope (6–8 feet) devoted to radial-velocity research in each hemisphere
rubrics_metrics.description: There is great need in both hemispheres of a huge reflecting telescope — six to eight feet in aperture — devoted almost exclusively to this research; one is in preparation at Mount Wilson for the northern hemisphere and a similar southern instrument is urged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate and plan for at least one very large dedicated reflector per hemisphere to carry out large-scale radial-velocity determinations for faint stars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete dataset per star for an ideal cosmical solution
rubrics_metrics.description: For the ideal solution to the riddle of the universe we need for every star: the proper motions (derived from plates/meridian work), the velocity in the line of sight (radial velocity), the parallax, the magnitude, and the spectrum-type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing survey requirements, aim to collect that full set of observables per star (proper motion, radial velocity, parallax, magnitude, spectrum type) to enable the most comprehensive cosmical analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance routine long-term labour with discovery-driven research
rubrics_metrics.description: The sole prosecution of routine labour, however high the ultimate object, would hardly be a healthy condition; the sense of progress is essential to healthy growth and new facts and discoveries are the best incentives to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a programme balance: while committing to long-term systematic data collection, include projects likely to yield new discoveries to sustain motivation and provide tests of accumulated work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pendulum gravity measurements and equipotential concept to infer geoid/earth shape
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief instrument of research for inferring the geoid (shape of earth's equipotential surface) is the pendulum: the time of vibration varies with place, from which gravity values are deduced and Stokes' method shows the geoid may be inferred from gravity variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply pendulum time-of-vibration measurements across locations and use established inversion methods (e.g., Stokes' approach) to infer the geoid; treat the geoid as the equipotential surface that runs underground beneath the continents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplification of continental/oceanic division by using a 1400-fathom contour
rubrics_metrics.description: If the sea were dried up, the contour-line at about 1400 fathoms would divide the surface into two regions of approximately equal area — the continental region and the oceanic region — simplifying the problem of modelling the Earth's form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modelling large-scale continental vs oceanic partitioning of Earth's surface, consider using the 1400-fathom bathymetric contour as a pragmatic separator to obtain a simplified, smoother geometry for dynamical analysis.
